title: Regression & Gradient Descent
oneLiner: Drawing the best straight line through messy data, and finding it by walking downhill.

what.html:
Regression means predicting a number. How much will this flat sell for? How long will this delivery take? How busy will a mobile tower be tonight?

You do it by looking at past examples and drawing the line that runs closest to all of them. Then you read new predictions off that line.

Everyday versionYou have taken twenty taxi rides and noted the distance and the fare for each. Plot them, lay a ruler through the middle of the dots, and you can estimate the fare for a ride you haven't taken yet. That ruler is a regression model.

The line has only two knobs: where it starts (its height at zero, the intercept) and how steep it is (the slope). Training a model just means finding the best setting for those knobs.

why.html:
• Nobody writes the rule for you. There's no formula for house prices, so we learn one from examples.
  • It's the fastest useful baseline. Before trying anything fancy, a straight line tells you how much signal is in the data.
  • The method carries over to everything else. "Score the guess, then nudge the knobs downhill" is exactly how deep neural networks are trained later. Learn it here and you've learned the engine.

how.title: Make a guess: a line with two knobs
how.html: Start with any line. Its prediction is price = start + slope × size. With more inputs (size, age, rooms) it's the same idea: each input gets its own knob, and the prediction is a weighted sum.

how.title: Score the guess: turn every miss into a square
how.html:
For each dot, measure how far the line misses it. Square that miss and add up all the squares. That total is the cost, one number that says how bad the line is.

Why squares? A miss of 4 counts as 16, not 4, so the line works hardest to avoid big misses. And squares never cancel out the way +3 and −3 would.

Try it: move the two knobs and watch the orange squares. Smallest total area wins.

how.title: Every knob setting has a score, and the scores form a bowl
how.html:
Imagine testing every possible slope and plotting the score for each. You get a valley shaped like a bowl, with exactly one lowest point. That bottom is the best line.

Why a bowl mattersA bowl has no false bottoms. Wherever you start, if you keep going downhill you reach the same best answer. (Neural networks are not this lucky. Their landscapes are bumpy.)

how.title: Shortcut: jump straight to the bottom
how.html:
For a straight line there's a formula, the normal equation, that computes the bottom of the bowl in one go. Think of it as solving the puzzle with algebra instead of trial and error.

It works well with a handful of inputs. With thousands of inputs the formula gets very slow, which is why we usually walk instead.

how.title: Or walk downhill in the fog
how.html:
Picture yourself on a foggy hillside. You can't see the valley, but you can feel which way the ground slopes under your feet. So you take a step downhill, feel again, and take another step.

That loop is gradient descent. The learning rate is your step size. Small steps are safe but slow. Steps that are too big carry you across the valley and up the other side.

One rule is worth remembering: if the error ever goes up, your steps are too big.

how.title: One step by hand (the exam question)
how.html:
Commonly quoted versions give a classic problem: three patients, heart-disease risk predicted from BMI and blood pressure, a starting line, and a step size of 0.02. "Do one step" means:

  1. Predict for each patient with the current line.
  2. Note each miss (prediction minus truth).
  3. Combine the misses into a downhill direction for each knob.
  4. Move each knob a small amount in that direction, all at once.

Interesting twist: because BMI and pressure are big numbers (30, 80, 100), even 0.02 is a huge step. After one step the error rises from 0.14 to about 209. The Deep Dive lets you replay it.

how.title: Ask everyone, a few, or one at a time
how.html:
To decide which way is downhill you can listen to all your data, a small group, or just one example.

  • Batch: survey the whole class before every decision. Accurate but slow.
  • Mini-batch: ask a table of 8 students. Quick and fairly reliable. This is the everyday choice.
  • Stochastic: ask one random student each time. Very fast, very jittery.

how.title: How good is the line?
how.html:
• Average miss (MAE): on average, how far off are we? Easy to explain to anyone.
  • RMSE: like the average miss, but big misses count extra.
  • R²: how much better are we than always guessing the average? 1 is perfect, 0 is no better than the average, and below 0 is worse.

Always judge on data the model has not seen.

how.title: Bending the line without breaking the method
how.html: If the true pattern curves, give the model extra ingredients: size², size³, and so on. The model is still a weighted sum of ingredients, so the same tools work. That's why it is still called a "linear" model even when the picture is curved.

how.title: Too simple vs too clever
how.html:
Too simple (underfitting): a straight ruler on a curved pattern. It misses everyone a bit.

Too clever (overfitting): a wiggly line that threads through every training dot, like a student who memorised last year's answers. Perfect on the practice exam, poor on the real one.

Fixes: more data, a simpler model, stopping training early, or a penalty (next step).

how.title: Keep the knobs on a leash: regularisation
how.html:
Add a penalty for large knob values to the score. The model now has to justify every big knob, so it stays smoother.

  • Ridge shrinks all knobs a little, like turning everyone's volume down.
  • Lasso switches some knobs fully off, which also tells you which inputs don't matter.
  • Elastic Net blends both.

In the demo above, raise the penalty slider with a high flexibility and watch the wiggles calm down.

demo.html:
This is gradient descent in one dimension. The curve is the error for each setting of a single knob. The ball is your current setting.

  • Learning rate 0.1–0.5: the ball rolls steadily into the valley.
  • Around 1.0: it lands almost exactly at the bottom in one jump. On this simple bowl that's the ideal step.
  • Between 1 and 2: it overshoots and zig-zags across the valley but still settles.
  • Above 2: every jump lands higher than the last. It diverges, which is what you'd see as error going up.

Click anywhere on the curve to drop the ball somewhere new.

example.html:
Forecasting how busy a mobile cell will be. An operator records, every hour, how many users are connected and how much data the cell carries. A regression line from "users" to "data volume" gives a quick forecast for tonight's peak.

When the forecast is above what the cell can handle, engineers can add capacity or rebalance traffic before customers notice slow speeds.

The same story shows up everywhere: delivery time from distance, electricity demand from temperature, salary from experience (the stated example).

misunderstandings: A bigger learning rate always trains faster.
Only up to a point. Past it, steps overshoot and the error grows. The demo above shows the exact tipping point.
A model that fits the training data perfectly is a great model.
Usually the opposite: it has memorised noise. Judge on unseen data.
'Linear' means it can only draw straight lines.
Linear refers to how the knobs combine (a weighted sum). Feed in x² and x³ and the curve bends.
The shortcut formula is always better because it's exact.
It gets very slow with many inputs and fails outright when inputs duplicate each other.
takeaways: Regression predicts a number by drawing the line closest to past examples.
The score of a line is the total of its squared misses. Lower is better, and the scores form a bowl.
Find the bottom with a one-shot formula (small problems) or by stepping downhill (big problems).
Step size matters: too small is slow, too large overshoots or blows up. If error rises, shrink it.
Too simple underfits, too flexible overfits. More data, simpler models, early stopping and penalties keep it honest.
thirty: Regression predicts a number, like a price, by fitting the line that runs closest to past data. We score a line by adding up its squared misses; the scores form a bowl with one lowest point. We can jump to the bottom with a formula, or walk downhill step by step with gradient descent, where the learning rate is the step size. We check the line on unseen data, and if it is too wiggly we add a penalty that keeps its knobs small.

check.q: You are training with gradient descent and the error goes up after every step. What should you do first?
check.why: Rising error means each step overshoots the valley. Smaller steps fix it.

check.q: Why do we square the misses instead of just adding them?
opts: So big misses count much more and positives and negatives don't cancel
Because computers can't add negative numbers
check.why: Squaring removes signs and punishes big misses heavily.

check.q: A wiggly model scores perfectly on training data but badly on new data. This is…
check.why: It memorised the training set instead of learning the pattern.

check.q: Which choice switches some inputs completely off?
check.why: Lasso can set knobs exactly to zero.

check.q: Asking one random example at a time which way is downhill is called…
check.why: Stochastic = one example per step: fast but jittery.
